say.text: A 68-year-old woman takes prednisolone and naproxen for arthritis. Since last night she has had sudden, severe epigastric pain.
Her abdomen is soft, with no board-like rigidity, but tender. Pulse 104. What do you do now?

choices.label: Observe overnight; no rigidity, so no perforation
Image now for free gas, before deciding
Discharge on analgesia; review in clinic
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Observing feels safe, because the rigidity you were taught to look for is missing.
But steroids and NSAIDs can blunt the peritoneal signs in older and steroid-treated patients, so missing rigidity cannot clear her.

sure_note.text: You were sure, and that is the risk: a confident soft-belly read in a steroid patient is how perforations get missed.

say.text: That choice is not right. Discharge is tempting, because she is comfortable on analgesia and her belly is soft.
But a soft belly in a steroid-treated patient is weak reassurance, because the signs can be blunted.

sure_note.text: You were sure she could go home. That confident error is exactly what this case is built to catch.

say.text: Ask first what steroids and naproxen do to the peritoneal signs. Then ask what that does to a soft belly.
Right: here is the reasoning. Her steroid and naproxen can blunt the peritoneal signs, so a soft belly does not settle it.
The classic rigid belly may never come in this patient, so imaging has to answer the question.
Other risks to know: smoking, H. pylori, and crack cocaine in younger patients.
Which statement about peritoneal signs in older or steroid-treated patients is correct?

choices.label: A soft belly can exclude perforation in older patients
Rigidity usually appears early; its absence makes it unlikely
Signs may be blunted; a soft belly does not exclude it
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a soft belly looks reassuring on examination, and older patients often look well.
But in older and steroid-treated patients the peritoneal signs are often blunted, so the examination is unreliable.

sure_note.text: You were sure a soft belly was enough. Confident errors on examination are the ones worth remembering.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because rigidity is the sign you were taught to trust, so its absence feels decisive.
But rigidity is blunted in these hosts, so its absence proves little, even though board-like rigidity is the classic picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure rigidity had to be there. That certainty is exactly what the host factors undo.

say.text: Ask which host factors dull the signs, then what a soft belly is worth in that host.
Right: here is the reasoning. Steroids, NSAIDs and age can blunt the peritoneal signs, so the examination is weak evidence.
A soft belly therefore does not settle the question; the picture and the investigation have to.
A man was admitted at midnight with a perforated ulcer. The night nurse hands over: his pain score has fallen from 9 to 3, and he is asking for tea.
What does that fall mean?

choices.label: A lull: the irritant is diluted, and bacteria may follow
Healing: the perforation is sealing as the pain eases
Settling: the acid has burned out, so the leak closes
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the pain has eased and he looks well, which reads like healing.
But the easing is the reaction stage: exudate dilutes the irritant while bacteria keep spreading.

sure_note.text: You were sure easing meant healing. That is the belief this case is built to catch.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the acid no longer hurts as it did, which looks like a burnt-out process.
But the acid is only the first stage: bacteria arrive over hours, and the quiet period is when they gain ground.

sure_note.text: You were sure the leak was closing. Read the quiet period as a stage, not as an end.

say.text: Ask what the fall in pain is made of: the acid itself, or the fluid that now dilutes it?
Right: here is the reasoning. Chemical peritonitis comes first, then the reaction stage, then bacterial peritonitis.
The fall in pain is dilution, not healing. The reaction stage can mislead the clinician into thinking he is improving.
Earlier he writhed on the trolley, rolling and pacing with colic-type pain. Now he lies motionless, knees drawn up, and winces when the bed is jolted.
What does the change mean?

choices.label: Colic settling: colic patients lie quietly once it passes
Peritonitis: movement now jars the inflamed peritoneum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because colic does pass, and a quiet patient looks like one who is settling.
But lying still and wincing at a jolt is the sign of peritonitis: movement worsens the peritoneal pain, which is why he lies still.

sure_note.text: You were sure colic had settled. Stillness with pain on jolting is the sign to read as peritonitis, not as calm.

say.text: Ask why he has stopped moving, and what movement does to an inflamed peritoneum.
Right: here is the reasoning. Movement worsens peritoneal pain, so the patient lies still and guards.
Board-like rigidity and sudden severe pain are the classic picture, so the stillness fits a perforation, not a settling colic.
A 35-year-old man has a 40 percent scald burn and is in intensive care. On day 3 a perforated duodenal ulcer is found.
Which stress ulcer is this?

choices.label: Cushing's ulcer, from the head injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two names are easy to swap, and both are stress ulcers.
But Cushing's ulcer is tied to the brain: raised intracranial pressure after head injury, not a burn.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the name, but the pair is swapped in memory. Anchor each eponym to its trigger.

say.text: Anchor each name to its trigger. Which of the two triggers is the burn?
Right: here is the reasoning. Burns give Curling's ulcer; head injury or raised intracranial pressure gives Cushing's.
These stress ulcers can perforate, so tying each name to its trigger is what stops the swap.
A 40-year-old man has a perforated ulcer. Fluid has tracked down the right paracolic gutter into the right iliac fossa.
His right-sided pain looks like appendicitis. Which eponym names this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because Kehr's is the eponym most often attached to shoulder-tip pain in the exam.
But Kehr's sign belongs to splenic rupture. Shoulder-tip pain in perforation is diaphragm irritation, and the fluid track has its own eponym.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a shoulder eponym, but that sign belongs to the spleen. Tie each eponym to the condition that owns it.

say.text: Ask which eponym describes fluid travelling down the gutter, rather than a referred pain.
Right: here is the reasoning. Gastric fluid tracking down the right paracolic gutter mimics appendicitis: Valentino's syndrome.
Shoulder-tip pain is a different thing, phrenic referral from the diaphragm, and it is not the eponym here.
